details:
VESTIBULAR GPS

A Personalized Approach to Monitoring Astronauts' Vestibular Health

Developed by Team MindStellar | NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

1. Why We Started This Project -

When we think about space exploration, we often think about rockets, spacecraft, and advanced technology. But behind every successful space mission, there is something equally important: the health and well-being of the astronauts.

Living and working in space is very different from living on Earth. Microgravity changes the way the human body responds to its surroundings, and one of the systems affected by these changes is the vestibular system.

The vestibular system, located in the inner ear, helps us maintain balance, understand our body position, and coordinate movement. On Earth, our brain uses information from the inner ear, eyes, and muscles to understand where we are and how we are moving. In space, microgravity changes this familiar environment, making it harder for the brain to interpret these signals in the usual way.

As a result, astronauts may experience dizziness, motion sickness, spatial disorientation, balance difficulties, and changes in movement coordination. These challenges can also continue after returning to Earth, when the body has to readjust to gravity.

While exploring this challenge, we started thinking about an important question:

How can we better understand and monitor the changes in an astronaut's balance and movement throughout a space mission?

That question became the starting point of VESTIBULAR GPS.

2. Understanding the Challenge -

The human body is naturally adapted to Earth's gravitational environment. However, during spaceflight, astronauts must adjust to conditions where gravity no longer provides the same familiar signals.

This adjustment can affect several aspects of their daily activities and physical performance.

Some of the major challenges include:

Balance Difficulties: Changes in vestibular signals may make it harder for astronauts to maintain balance and control their body movements.

Spatial Disorientation: Astronauts may have difficulty understanding their body position, direction, and movement in an unfamiliar environment.

Sensorimotor Changes: The brain needs to adapt to new patterns of sensory information, which may affect coordination between perception and physical movement.

Space Motion Sickness: Changes in sensory information can contribute to nausea, dizziness, and general discomfort, especially during the early stages of adaptation.

Readaptation After Returning to Earth: After spending time in microgravity, astronauts may temporarily experience difficulties with walking, standing, and maintaining balance as their bodies readjust to Earth's gravity.

Another important thing we considered is that these experiences are not the same for every astronaut. People have different physical abilities, previous performance levels, and adaptation patterns.

This means that comparing everyone against the same general standard may not always provide the full picture of an individual's progress or changes.

We wanted to explore a more personalized way of monitoring these differences.

3. Introducing Our Solution: VESTIBULAR GPS -

VESTIBULAR GPS is an offline, browser-based system developed to monitor changes in astronauts' balance, movement, and sensorimotor performance through repeated assessment sessions.

The main idea behind our project is simple:

Every astronaut is different, so why should everyone be evaluated using exactly the same reference standard?

Instead of depending only on general population standards, VESTIBULAR GPS focuses on an astronaut's own performance history.

The system uses information from previous assessment sessions to establish a personalized baseline. When new assessment results become available, they can be compared with that baseline to identify possible changes over time.

For example, if an astronaut completes an assessment before a mission and repeats it after spending time in microgravity, the system can help show how their performance has changed compared with their own earlier results.

The results are presented through a visual dashboard, along with confidence information that helps users understand how reliably the available results should be interpreted.

We designed VESTIBULAR GPS to make performance monitoring more personal, understandable, and accessible.

It is intended to support health monitoring and assessment, not to replace medical professionals or provide a clinical diagnosis.

4. Who Is VESTIBULAR GPS For?

Although astronauts are our primary focus, we believe the concept could also be useful to the people who work behind the scenes to keep astronauts healthy and safe.

Astronauts: The system is designed to help monitor individual changes in balance, movement, and sensorimotor performance across different assessment sessions.

Flight Surgeons and Medical Teams: The monitoring information could help medical professionals observe performance changes and support further health assessments.

Researchers and Scientists: Researchers studying vestibular adaptation, neuroscience, human physiology, and the effects of microgravity could benefit from observing performance patterns over time.

Space Agencies and Mission Planners: The concept could contribute to future astronaut health-monitoring systems, particularly for longer missions to the Moon and Mars.

Our aim is to make the information useful not only for monitoring astronauts but also for understanding how the human body adapts to space.

5. How Does It Work?

We wanted to keep the basic idea of VESTIBULAR GPS straightforward: collect assessment information, understand individual performance, compare changes, and present the results clearly.

The system follows these steps:

Step 1 – Assessment

An astronaut completes the available assessment activities, which collect information related to balance, movement, and sensorimotor performance.

Step 2 – Building a Personal Baseline

The system uses previous assessment sessions to establish an individual reference point. This baseline represents the astronaut's own performance history.

Step 3 – Comparing Performance

New assessment results are compared with the astronaut's previous baseline. This helps identify differences between earlier and current performance.

Step 4 – Identifying Changes

The system highlights possible changes and variations across assessment sessions, making it easier to observe performance patterns over time.

Step 5 – Understanding Confidence

Along with performance information, the system communicates confidence levels. This gives users additional context when interpreting the results and reminds them that not every measurement has the same level of certainty.

Step 6 – Viewing Results

The dashboard brings the information together in a visual and organized format, helping users understand the astronaut's performance history.

Through these steps, VESTIBULAR GPS aims to turn repeated assessment information into something easier to follow and understand.

6. What Makes VESTIBULAR GPS Useful?

While developing the project, we focused on features that could make the monitoring process more practical and meaningful.
1. Personalized Baselines: Uses an individual's previous assessment sessions as a reference rather than relying only on general standards.
2. Performance Comparison: Helps identify changes between different assessment sessions.
3. Balance and Movement Monitoring: Focuses on vestibular-related performance and sensorimotor changes.
4. Confidence Information: Provides additional context to help users interpret assessment results.
5. Visual Dashboard: Presents information in an organized and understandable way.
6. Offline Functionality: Designed to work through a browser without depending on continuous internet connectivity.
7. Individual-Focused Monitoring: Recognizes that every astronaut may respond differently to microgravity.

Together, these features reflect our effort to make astronaut performance monitoring more personalized and accessible.

7. What Makes Our Approach Different?

One of the main ideas we wanted to bring into this project is the importance of looking at individual changes rather than relying entirely on general comparisons.

Imagine two astronauts completing the same assessment. They may naturally have different balance abilities and movement patterns even before entering space. Comparing their results with each other may not always explain how each person is adapting.

Now imagine comparing each astronaut's current performance with their own previous results.

This gives a different perspective.

For us, that is the most important idea behind VESTIBULAR GPS. We want to focus on how an individual changes over time, not simply how they compare with someone else.

We also considered the practical challenges of space missions. Internet connectivity cannot always be assumed in every environment, so we developed the system with offline accessibility in mind.

By bringing together personalized baselines, session comparisons, confidence information, and visual monitoring, we aim to offer a more individual-focused approach to understanding vestibular-related performance.

8. Expected Benefits and Future Impact

We understand that a monitoring system alone cannot eliminate the physical challenges astronauts experience in space. However, having a clearer picture of performance changes can be an important step toward better assessment and support.

VESTIBULAR GPS aims to:
1. Help identify possible changes in vestibular-related performance over time.
2. Support medical teams in understanding individual adaptation patterns.
3. Provide a clearer picture of performance before, during, and after exposure to microgravity, where assessment data is available.
4. Make it easier to compare repeated assessment sessions.
5. Support research into balance, spatial orientation, and sensorimotor adaptation.
6. Encourage more personalized approaches to astronaut health monitoring.

Looking ahead, we believe this approach could be particularly relevant as space missions become longer and more complex.

Future missions to the Moon and Mars will require a better understanding of how the human body responds to unfamiliar gravitational environments. We hope VESTIBULAR GPS can contribute to that growing area of research.

9. Tools and Technologies

We developed VESTIBULAR GPS as an offline, browser-based software solution.

Our development process brought together research, software development, data interpretation, and interface design.

The system uses web-based technologies to organize assessment information, compare performance across sessions, and present results through a visual dashboard.

We also focused on keeping the system accessible through a browser without requiring continuous internet connectivity.

For our team, the goal was not simply to build another dashboard. We wanted to create something that connects a real challenge in human space exploration with a practical, understandable technological approach.

10. What We Considered During Development

Throughout the development process, we kept several important factors in mind.

Individual Differences: We recognized that astronauts have different physical abilities and performance histories. This is why personalization became the central idea of our project.

Effects of Microgravity: We considered how unfamiliar gravitational conditions can influence balance, spatial orientation, and movement coordination.

Accessibility: We wanted the system to be straightforward to access and understand.

Limited Connectivity: Since continuous internet access cannot always be guaranteed in space environments, we considered offline functionality an important part of the design.

Responsible Interpretation: We considered the importance of presenting confidence information and avoiding the assumption that every change represents a medical problem.

Future Possibilities: We designed the concept with the possibility of future development, testing, and integration with additional assessment technologies in mind.

11. Limitations and What We Hope to Improve

Like any developing technology, VESTIBULAR GPS has room for improvement.

At this stage, it is a prototype intended to support personalized monitoring of vestibular-related performance. It has not been established as a clinically validated diagnostic system, and its results should not be used independently to determine an astronaut's medical condition or fitness for a mission.

We believe that further research and testing will be necessary to understand how effectively this approach can work in real spaceflight conditions.

In the future, we hope to explore:
1. Integration with validated vestibular assessment protocols.
2. Additional physiological and movement sensors.
3. Testing in simulated microgravity environments.
4. Integration with relevant astronaut health datasets.
5. Collaboration with space medicine professionals and researchers.
6. Further improvement of performance comparison and confidence methods.

These steps could help us develop the current prototype into a more comprehensive monitoring solution.

12. Our Vision

For us, VESTIBULAR GPS is more than a software project. It is an attempt to address a human challenge behind the future of space exploration.

We brought together our interests in psychology, neuroscience, research, and technology to explore how we might better understand the changes astronauts experience in microgravity.

We know that space exploration is not only about reaching new destinations. It is also about making sure that the people who take us there can remain healthy, safe, and capable of adapting to the challenges they face.

Through VESTIBULAR GPS, we hope to contribute to a future where astronaut health monitoring becomes more personalized, accessible, and meaningful.

Because every astronaut has a different journey, we believe every journey deserves a personalized way to understand and monitor human adaptation.
